fields.meta_title: 404 Page Examples and Best Practices | Emergent
fields.meta_description: A 404 page tells visitors a URL doesn't exist. See 404 page examples by site type and the status code rules, then build yours from a prompt.
fields.h1: Build a 404 Page That Finds the Next Page
fields.hero_description: Describe your site and Emergent builds the 404 page behind it, with search over your own content and a table of every URL that missed.
fields.features_subheading: Describe the site once and Emergent writes the page, the data behind it and the code you keep.
fields.feature_1:
A status code you ask for by name

Your prompt names the code: unknown URLs answer with a 404 and the designed page. Crawlers read the code; people read the page. Test the response on a made-up address before you send traffic to the site.
fields.feature_2:
Search over your own pages

A search box on the error page queries your own products or docs. Words from the broken URL prefill the box, and a visitor who mistyped one letter is a click away.
fields.feature_3:
Every miss saved as a row

Each missed URL lands as a row in a database you own, the same one behind the rest of your app. Query it whenever you like or wire it to a weekly report, with no analytics script from another vendor in between.
fields.feature_4:
Your own navigation and footer

Your site navigation and footer stay on the error page, in your own fonts and colors. Visitors can tell they never left, and the menu they already know stays one glance away.
fields.feature_5:
Copy in the voice you describe

Emergent writes the heading and the next-step links in the voice your prompt sets out. Describe that voice in a sentence, then edit any line before the page goes live.
fields.feature_6:
Code you keep

The 404 page and its miss log export to your GitHub repository. Host them on Emergent under your custom domain, or deploy the code wherever the rest of your site already runs.

fields.usecase_heading: 404 Pages for Four Kinds of Site
fields.tab_content_1:
A dead product link that still sells

A shopper who follows an old link to Northwind's retired linen camp shirt lands on a page that keeps the store open. Search sits at the top, with the store's bestsellers below it and an add-to-cart button on each. An add from the error page is saved with the missed URL attached.
fields.tab_content_2:
Search seeded from the broken URL

Acme's API docs collect mistyped links from forum posts and old emails. When /docs/api/webhoks misses, the 404 splits the path into words and searches the docs. The closest article comes first: Webhooks: retries and signatures. A link to the docs home and a support email sit under the result.
fields.tab_content_3:
Let the joke carry a link back to the work

Fernhill is a design studio, and its visitors come to see projects. Its 404 opens with one line, "This page is out sketching," and one button, Show me a random project, that loads a case study from the portfolio. A plain homepage link sits under the button for anyone who wants the full menu.
fields.tab_content_4:
Which old URLs need a redirect this week

Site migrations leave old addresses alive in newsletters and other people's posts. After Globex moved its marketing site, each 404 hit lands in a table with the URL, the referrer and a seven-day count. Every Monday, a Slack post to the web team lists the URLs with 20 or more hits as candidates for a 301 redirect.

fields.howto_description: A 404 page has one job: get someone who hit a dead address to the next page worth opening. These seven steps cover what goes on the page and what to check once it is live, and Emergent builds the result from a description of your site.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Find where your misses come from
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Write the heading in plain words
fields.howto_step_1_des: Start with the source of your broken links: retired products, mistyped docs URLs or addresses from an old site. The source decides what the page leads with: a search box for typos, products for a store, a pointer for a move.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Admit the miss in one short heading, then name the likely cause, such as an outdated link, without blaming the visitor. Keep the error code in small type below it; the heading and the next step do the work.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Put a search box near the top and two or three links under it: the homepage, your most visited section and a way to contact you. On a store, show products in stock; on a docs site, the closest article.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Keep the error page lean. Drop pop-ups and sign-up forms that compete with the way out, and click every link on it before launch, because a 404 page with a broken link of its own sends visitors in a circle.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Save each 404 hit with the requested URL and its referrer. The referrer column tells a one-off typo apart from a partner site whose broken link sends you traffic every day.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Check the status code before launch
fields.howto_step_6_des: Request an address that never existed and read the response in your browser's network tab. It should say 404. A 200 on an error page is a soft 404, and Google keeps it out of Search.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Sort the miss log by hits once a week. A URL whose content moved gets a 301 to its new address. For a page you removed on purpose, answer with 410 Gone, which MDN defines as a permanent removal. Check the list again after any release that renames pages.

claims_to_source: A 404 status says the server cannot find the resource, without saying whether the absence is temporary or permanent; 410 Gone marks a permanent removal
A soft 404 is an error page that returns a 200 status, and Google excludes it from Search
Google does not index URLs that return 4xx codes and removes ones already indexed
A page that moved should return a 301 permanent redirect to its new URL
404 errors on URLs that never existed or were removed do not hurt how the rest of a site ranks
Government guidance for 404 pages: plain, non-technical language, a search bar, next steps, no whimsy where users need critical services
GitHub Pages serves a 404.html file at the root of the repository as the site's custom 404 page
Search Console's Page Indexing report lists URLs that returned Not found (404)

scope.evidence: H1 'Build a 404 Page That Finds the Next Page', meta 'Examples and Best Practices' and hero cover the page, its search and its miss log.

intent.evidence: Definition up top for the AI Overview (FAQ 1), status-code rules from MDN and Google that the galleries skip (feature_1, howto_step_6), four examples by site type, and 9 PAA questions answered.

specificity.evidence: Web-team vocabulary: '410', 'soft 404', 'referrer', 'seven-day count', '/docs/api/webhoks', 'Page Indexing report', 'a 301 redirect'.

openers.evidence: Five feature bodies open on subjectless fragments (CONTENT_DEFECTS #2, #16): 'Puts a search box', 'Writes each missed URL', 'Keeps your site navigation', 'Generates the heading', 'Exports the 404 page'.

craft.evidence: Ideas restated across fields (CONTENT_DEFECTS #21): tone by site type (feature_5, howto_step_4, FAQ 7), header/footer/fonts (feature_4, howto_step_4), sort the miss log by hits for redirects (feature_3, howto_step_5, howto_step_7), admit the miss (howto_description, howto_step_2, FAQ 1), old links in newsletters (tab_content_4, FAQ 3).

voice.evidence: Plain and exact: 'Crawlers read the code; people read the page.' 'This page is out sketching.' No AI tells or hype.

truth.evidence: Emergent hosting returning a real 404 status is not in the capability ledger (feature_1 'Emergent sets the route for unknown URLs to answer with a 404 code'); fields contradict on 410 (feature_1 and howto_step_6 versus howto_step_7 'one that is gone for good stays a 404'); unsourced generalizations (FAQ 2 'Every host has a setting for it.', FAQ 9 'That visibility made 404 shorthand for missing').

distinct.evidence: Own page: store, API docs, studio, migration; thank-you and landing-page-seo siblings are linked, not mirrored.

faq.evidence: FAQ 6 restates howto_step_6 (CONTENT_DEFECTS #21): 'Open the network tab in your browser's developer tools ... The response should read 404; a 200 means...' versus 'read the response in your browser's network tab. It should say 404 ... A 200 on an error page is a soft 404'.

images.evidence: Tab 1 sells the retired product: the page reads 'This shirt has left the shop' for /products/linen-camp-shirt, then offers 'Linen camp shirt, sage, $68, in stock' with Add to cart, against copy 'Northwind's retired linen camp shirt' (CONTENT_DEFECTS #20).

findings.quote: Emergent sets the route for unknown URLs to answer with a 404 code and your designed page, or a 410 for content removed on purpose.
findings.issue: Whether an Emergent-hosted app answers an unknown URL with a non-200 status is a guarantee about Emergent's own hosting, not something a prompt controls; no capability ledger entry covers it (claims_used lists only prompt-build, database-owned, code-export, custom-domain, api-connect). Every instance: features_subheading 'Emergent builds the error page, the status code it returns'; feature_1 (quoted); why_description 'Emergent builds one that returns the right status'; FAQ 2 'you describe the page and get the design and the routing in one build, with the 404 status set'; tab_content_1 'gets a 404 status'; tab_image_1 chip 'Status 404 returned'.
findings.fix: Divit decides whether to add a ledger entry for hosted status codes. Until then, phrase it as an instruction plus a test: 'Ask for unknown URLs to return a 404 status (or 410 for removed content), then check the response before launch', which howto_step_6 already teaches. Drop the status chip from tab 1 or relabel it.

findings.quote: one that is gone for good stays a 404
findings.issue: This contradicts feature_1 'or a 410 for content removed on purpose' and howto_step_6_des 'or 410 for content you removed for good'. MDN (the recorded source) gives 410 Gone for permanent removal.
findings.fix: 'one that is gone for good returns a 404 or a 410' (or a 410 alone), consistent with feature_1 and step 6.

findings.quote: Every host has a setting for it.
findings.issue: An unsupported generalization (FAQ 2). Same class in FAQ 9: 'Most HTTP errors happen out of sight, but a 404 appears on screen whenever a link points nowhere. Every site produces some. That visibility made 404 shorthand for missing' (unsourced causal and historical claims); FAQ 3 'Links in newsletters and on other sites go on sending people to a URL long after it changes.' is plausible but unsourced.
findings.fix: FAQ 2: 'Most hosts let you set one; on GitHub Pages, a file named 404.html...' FAQ 9: source the history (the Wikipedia HTTP 404 article in the top 10 is a start) or answer with what is verifiable: a 404 is the error people actually see on screen, so sites design for it.

findings.quote: This shirt has left the shop ... Linen camp shirt, sage $68, in stock ... Add to cart
findings.issue: The copy says the linen camp shirt is retired; the image says it has left the shop, then sells the same shirt as an in-stock bestseller, and the 'Added to cart' card pairs the missed URL with that same item. Copy also says 'bestsellers ... an add-to-cart button on each' (plural); one is drawn.
findings.fix: Show a different bestseller (for example 'Oxford shirt, navy, $72') and at least two bestseller rows, so the cart card shows another product added from the retired shirt's URL.

findings.quote: Puts a search box on the error page that queries your own products or docs.
findings.issue: Subjectless fragments open five feature bodies: feature_2 'Puts a search box...'; feature_3 'Writes each missed URL to a database you own...'; feature_4 'Keeps your site navigation and footer...'; feature_5 'Generates the heading and the next-step links...'; feature_6 'Exports the 404 page and its miss log...'. The row #16 fix names its subject ('Emergent generates...'), and approved pages use subjects or imperatives.
findings.fix: Give each a subject or make it an imperative, varied across the six: 'A search box on the error page queries your own products or docs.' 'Every missed URL lands in a database you own...' 'Ask for the copy in the tone you want...'

findings.quote: Keep it plain for a bank or a clinic, or write a joke for a studio site whose visitors came to browse.
findings.issue: Tone by site type is restated in howto_step_4_des 'decide the tone up front: plain for services people rely on, lighter for a portfolio or a game' and FAQ 7 'Skip the humor on sites people need for critical services.'
findings.fix: Keep the rule once (FAQ 7, with the sourced USWDS guidance); feature_5 and howto_step_4 say something new.

findings.quote: Keeps your site navigation and footer on the error page, in your own fonts and colors.
findings.issue: Restated in howto_step_4_des 'Wrap the error message in the same header and footer as every other page. Match the fonts and colors'.
findings.fix: One field owns it; the other moves on (for example, howto_step_4 covers what to keep out of the error page's navigation).

findings.quote: Sort by hits and the broken links worth fixing first rise to the top, each a candidate for a redirect.
findings.issue: Sort the miss log by hits and redirect the top ones is said in feature_3, howto_step_5_des 'Save each 404 hit with the requested URL and its referrer in a table you can sort. A weekly count by URL...', howto_step_7_des 'Sort the miss log by hits once a week. A URL whose content moved gets a 301' and tab_content_4 (the worked example).
findings.fix: Tab 4 is the example and howto_step_7 the instruction; feature_3 describes the log itself, and howto_step_5 merges into step 7 or covers what to log.

findings.quote: A useful 404 page admits the address is wrong
findings.issue: Restated in howto_step_2_des 'Admit the miss in one short heading' and FAQ 1 'A good 404 error page admits the miss in plain words, then offers search or a link'.
findings.fix: Keep it in howto_step_2; howto_description and FAQ 1 say something else.

findings.quote: Site migrations leave old addresses alive in newsletters and other people's posts.
findings.issue: Restated in FAQ 3 'Links in newsletters and on other sites go on sending people to a URL long after it changes.'
findings.fix: Cut the FAQ 3 sentence; its earlier causes already answer the question.

findings.quote: Open the network tab in your browser's developer tools as you do it. The response should read 404; a 200 means the site serves its error page as if it were a normal one.
findings.issue: FAQ 6 restates howto_step_6_des 'read the response in your browser's network tab. It should say 404 ... A 200 on an error page is a soft 404', and FAQ 10 repeats it again ('a soft 404 that answers 200').
findings.fix: FAQ 6 answers how to find another site's 404 page (the made-up path) and stops; the status check stays in howto_step_6.
